title: Communication methods & tailoring the message
blurb: Know the range of communication methods (face to face, written, virtual; push, pull, interactive) and tailor each message to its audience.
question: A university's new student records system will go live two weeks late. The project manager has to tell the university's board, the administrative staff who will use the system, and thousands of students. Which methods should be used, and how should the message differ for each group?

teach.h: Many ways to send a message
teach.body: Communication methods fall into three broad families: face to face (meetings, workshops, one-to-ones), written or physical (reports, letters, newsletters, notice boards) and virtual (email, video and phone conferencing, messaging, collaboration platforms, intranets, social media). Each can be formal or informal, and push, pull or interactive. Tailoring means adapting the content, detail, language, format and channel of a message to each stakeholder's needs, interest, influence and preferences.

rows.label: Weakness
values: No proof it was read or understood

teach.h: Strengths and limits of each family
Formal and informal both have a place
teach.body: Formal communication (signed approvals, minutes, reports, contracts) creates a record and an audit trail, which governance needs. Informal communication (a chat by the coffee machine, a quick message) is fast and builds relationships, but it leaves weak traceability. Good practice combines them: talk it through for speed and understanding, then confirm decisions in writing. Choosing a method means weighing the audience, purpose, urgency, sensitivity, complexity and whether a record is needed.

A message only works if the receiver finds it relevant and can understand it. Sending everyone the same detailed report means executives skim past what they need, users drown in technical terms and some groups never open it. Tailoring uses the stakeholder analysis: powerful but busy people get short, decision-focused summaries; users get practical 'what this means for you'; specialists get the detail. The facts stay the same; the framing, depth and channel change.

Content and detail
Channel
rows: New training dates, what changes for them
teach.caption: Same facts, four tailored messages. Each channel matches how that group prefers to receive and respond.

teach.h: Methods in linear and iterative projects

rows.label: Emphasis
values: Face to face and visible progress

teach.caption: Both need tailoring; iterative projects lean on interactive methods because feedback drives each iteration.

teach.text: 'I emailed everyone, so it has been communicated' is the classic mistake. Sending is not the same as understanding. Urgent, sensitive or complex messages need an interactive method; decisions that must be evidenced need a formal written record. Also beware the distractor that the most detailed report suits everyone: it suits almost no one.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name a method from the right family (face to face, written or virtual) and say whether it is push, pull or interactive.
Justify it against the situation: audience, urgency, sensitivity, complexity, need for a record.
Give one strength and one limitation of the method you chose.
Explain how you would tailor content, detail, language, format or channel to that stakeholder.
Show the payoff: relevant messages lead to understanding, engagement and support.
Families: face to face, written or physical, virtual.
Formal gives a record; informal gives speed and rapport. Confirm talk in writing.
Tailor content, detail, language, format and channel to each stakeholder.
Choose by audience, purpose, urgency, sensitivity, complexity and record needed.

summary: You can now describe the range of communication methods, classify them as push, pull or interactive, and weigh their strengths and limits. You can also explain why and how a message is tailored to different stakeholders, and choose a fitting method for a given situation.

A.q: Which of the following is an example of PULL communication?
options: A weekly email to the board
A phone call to a supplier
A.why: Pull communication is posted where people can fetch it when they choose, such as an intranet page or shared site.

whyNot.0: An email is sent to named recipients, so it is push.
whyNot.1: A phone call is two-way and real time, so it is interactive.
whyNot.3: A workshop is interactive: people exchange views in real time.

A.q: A project manager must tell a team member that their role on the project is ending. Which method is most appropriate?
options: A post on the team chat channel
An item in the project newsletter
An update on the notice board
A.why: Sensitive personal news needs a private, face-to-face conversation where the person can react and ask questions.

whyNot.1: A team chat post is public and impersonal for sensitive personal news.
whyNot.2: A newsletter is broadcast to many readers and gives the person no chance to respond privately.
whyNot.3: A notice board is public and one-way: entirely wrong for personal news.

A.q: Tailoring communication means adapting which of the following to each stakeholder?
options: Only the date the message is sent
The project's scope and its budget
The facts, so that each group is pleased
A.why: Tailoring adapts content, detail, language, format and channel to each stakeholder's needs, interest, influence and preferences.

whyNot.0: Timing matters, but tailoring covers much more than the send date.
whyNot.1: Scope and budget are project decisions, not things you change to suit an audience.
whyNot.2: Tailoring changes how a message is framed, never the facts themselves.

B.q: What is the main strength of formal written communication on a project?
B.why: Formal written communication creates a permanent, auditable record of decisions and approvals.

whyNot.0: Written communication is slow and one-way; instant feedback is a strength of interactive methods.
whyNot.2: Sensitive personal news is better handled face to face.
whyNot.3: Rapport builds fastest through face-to-face and informal contact.

B.q: Which statement best describes INTERACTIVE communication?
options: Information is posted for people to find
Messages are sent out to a defined list
Reports are filed away ready for a later audit
Two or more parties exchange in real time
B.why: Interactive communication is a real-time, two-way exchange, such as a meeting, phone call or video conference.

whyNot.0: Posting information for people to find describes pull communication.
whyNot.1: Sending to a defined list describes push communication.
whyNot.2: Filing reports is record-keeping, not an exchange between people.

B.q: A non-specialist councillor with high power must approve a technical design choice on a bridge project. What is the best way to present it?
options: A link to the project file store
B.why: Tailoring for a powerful non-specialist means plain language focused on the impacts and the decision needed.

whyNot.1: Engineering drawings are pitched at specialists and are hard for a non-specialist to interpret.
whyNot.2: A specification is too technical and doesn't highlight the decision or its impacts.
whyNot.3: A file link is pull communication with no tailoring and no guidance on what matters.

C.q:
Which THREE are virtual communication methods?
1. Video conferencing
2. Notice boards
3. Collaboration platforms
4. Instant messaging
C.why: Video conferencing, collaboration platforms and instant messaging are all virtual. Notice boards are a written or physical method.

whyNot.0: Notice boards are physical, not virtual, and instant messaging is missing.
whyNot.1: Notice boards are physical, not virtual, and collaboration platforms are missing.
whyNot.3: Notice boards are physical, not virtual, and video conferencing is missing.

C.q: On an iterative project, the sponsor wants to see real progress without attending the team's daily stand-ups. Which method best suits this?
options: A formal report at project closure
C.why: Iteration reviews show working output and invite feedback, at a frequency that suits a senior stakeholder.

whyNot.0: The sponsor has said they don't want to attend stand-ups, which are team coordination sessions.
whyNot.2: Code is far too technical and isn't tailored to a sponsor's needs.
whyNot.3: A closure report comes far too late to show progress or allow steering.

C.q: A project manager announces a major office relocation only by email. Staff react with anxiety and many questions. What would have been the best approach?
options: Send a longer, more detailed email
Post the plan on the intranet only
Wait until staff ask questions before replying
Brief staff in person, then follow up
C.why: A big, emotive change needs interactive communication so concerns are heard and answered, backed by a written follow-up for the record.

whyNot.0: More detail in the same one-way channel won't address anxiety or allow questions.
whyNot.1: Intranet-only is pull communication and still gives no chance for dialogue.
whyNot.2: Waiting lets rumour and anxiety grow; communication should be proactive.

reteach.title: Running a music festival
reteach.question: A festival has to tell ticket holders, stage crew, the council's licensing team and the neighbouring village that the main stage times have changed. Would one method work for all of them?

blocks.body: Ticket holders get a push notification in the festival app and the new times on screens around the site. Stage crew hear it on their radios, where they can ask questions instantly. The licensing team receive a formal letter, because it may affect the licence and needs a record. Villagers get a leaflet and a website update about later noise. Same news, tailored and sent the way each group needs it.

blocks.text: A radio call to the licensing team would be quick but leave no record; a formal letter to the stage crew would arrive too late to be useful. The right method depends on the audience and the purpose.

explain.body: Face to face: meetings, workshops, one-to-ones. Written or physical: reports, letters, newsletters, notice boards. Virtual: email, video and phone conferencing, messaging, collaboration platforms, intranets and social media. Most projects use a mix of all three.

explain.caption: A report or newsletter can be printed or sent electronically.

test.q: Which of these is a written or physical method rather than a virtual one?
test.why: A printed newsletter is a physical, written method.

whyNot.0: Video conferencing is a virtual method.
whyNot.2: Instant messaging is a virtual method.
whyNot.3: An intranet is a virtual method.

explain.body: Push sends information to specific people (email, letters, reports) but doesn't prove it was read or understood. Pull posts it for people to fetch (intranet, shared site, dashboard), which suits large audiences but relies on them looking. Interactive is two-way in real time (meetings, calls, workshops) and is best for understanding and agreement.

explain.caption: Moving right, feedback and understanding increase, but so does the time needed.

test.q: What is the main weakness of PUSH communication such as email?
options: It leaves no record at all
It needs everyone in the same room at once
test.why: Push messages arrive, but there's no built-in check that they were read or understood.

whyNot.0: Push methods like email can reach very large lists.
whyNot.1: Email and letters usually do leave a record.
whyNot.2: Push methods don't need people together; that's a feature of face-to-face meetings.

explain.body: Formal communication (approvals, minutes, reports) creates the record governance and audits need. Informal communication is quick and builds relationships but is hard to trace. A sound habit: agree things in conversation, then confirm them in a short written summary.

test.q: Why might a project manager follow a verbal agreement with a short written summary?
options: To keep a record of what was agreed
To avoid any further conversation about it
To replace the need for a meeting
test.why: The conversation gives speed and understanding; the written summary adds a formal record.

whyNot.1: The aim is a record, not shutting down conversation.
whyNot.2: The meeting has already happened; the summary records it.
whyNot.3: Putting it in writing makes it more formal, not less.

explain.body: Tailoring adapts content, detail, language, format and channel to each stakeholder's needs, interest, influence and preferences, using the stakeholder analysis. Executives want brief, decision-focused summaries; users want practical impact; specialists want detail. The facts never change, only how they are presented.

test.q: Which factor from stakeholder analysis should most shape how much DETAIL a message contains?
options: The project's chosen life cycle approach
The size of the project budget
test.why: Detail is tailored to what the stakeholder needs to know and how interested they are.

whyNot.0: Location affects channel and timing, not depth.
whyNot.1: The life cycle shapes the rhythm of communication, not each stakeholder's level of detail.
whyNot.3: Budget size doesn't tell you how much detail a particular person needs.
